sourceEvidence.claim: Footnotes a and b — the watershed-area definition and the most vulnerable neurons (Purkinje cells; pyramidal cells of hippocampus and neocortex, layers 3, 5, 6)
sourceEvidence.quote:
a

Watershed areas (border zones) receive blood supply from most distal branches of 2 arteries with
limited collateral vascularity. These areas are susceptible to ischemia from hypoperfusion.
b
Neurons most vulnerable to hypoxic-ischemic insults include Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and
pyramidal cells of the hippocampus and neocortex (layers 3, 5, 6).

sourceEvidence.claim: Free radical injury — the three damages, the initiators (radiation, phase I metabolism, redox, nitric oxide, transition metals via Fenton, WBC oxidative burst), and the eliminators (catalase, SOD, glutathione peroxidase, spontaneous decay, vitamins A/C/E, transferrin, ceruloplasmin)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Free radical injury

Free radicals damage cells via membrane lipid peroxidation, protein modification, DNA breakage.
Initiated via radiation exposure (eg, cancer therapy), metabolism of drugs (phase I), redox
reactions, nitric oxide (eg, inflammation), transition metals (eg, iron, copper; form free radicals
via Fenton reaction), WBC (eg, neutrophils, macrophages) oxidative burst.
Free radicals can be eliminated by scavenging enzymes (eg, catalase, superoxide dismutase,
glutathione peroxidase), spontaneous decay, antioxidants (eg, vitamins A, C, E), and certain metal
carrier proteins (eg, transferrin, ceruloplasmin).
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: The three example groups — oxygen toxicity (ROP, BPD, post-thrombolytic reperfusion); drug/chemical toxicity (acetaminophen; CCl4 → P-450 → CCl3 → fatty liver with ↓ apolipoprotein synthesis, centrilobular necrosis); metal storage diseases (hemochromatosis iron, Wilson copper)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Examples:
▘ Oxygen toxicity: retinopathy of prematurity (abnormal vascularization), bronchopulmonary
dysplasia, reperfusion injury after thrombolytic therapy
▘ Drug/chemical toxicity: acetaminophen overdose (hepatotoxicity), carbon tetrachloride
(converted by cytochrome P-450 into CCl3 free radical → fatty liver [cell injury
→ ↓ apolipoprotein synthesis → fatty change], centrilobular necrosis)
▘ Metal storage diseases: hemochromatosis (iron) and Wilson disease (copper)
